title: Streaming parameter validator and human-friendly error envelope
creator: Marco Alvarez
description:
Goal: design and implement a streaming-aware JSON schema definition and validator for function/tool calls that emits incremental validation feedback, a compact human-friendly error envelope, and a compatibility layer that adapts legacy call shapes (v1) to the new strict/annotated schema (v2).

Background: current tool/function calling validates only at final payload arrival and returns dense machine-oriented errors. This causes poor developer UX in streaming scenarios (long-running responses) and brittle integrations when callers send older/variant parameter shapes. We need a validator that: (1) can run in partial/streaming mode and surface early, actionable hints; (2) produces deterministic, localized error codes and user-friendly messages; (3) supports runtime coercion modes and a compatibility transform chain for legacy clients; (4) integrates with telemetry and rollback-safe rollouts.

Proposed design summary: implement a validator component with three logical layers (all represented as configuration or lightweight rules so they can be rolled back without model changes):
- Schema format: JSON Schema subset + annotations for streaming semantics. Annotations include: "streamable": ["paramA","paramB"], "preferred_coercion": "lossy|strict|suggest", and "compat_aliases": {"oldField": "newField"}. Keep subset intentionally small (types, required, enum, pattern, min/max) and permit per-field streaming hints (e.g., "canValidatePrefix": true).
- Streaming validation lifecycle: the validator accepts partial objects and emits events: VALID_PART, HINT, SOFT_ERROR, HARD_ERROR. VALID_PART and HINT are informational and non-fatal; SOFT_ERROR includes suggested fixes/coercions and a confidence score; HARD_ERROR blocks invocation. For streaming flows, the runtime will surface HINT/SOFT_ERROR to the caller (if client opts in) and will continue to accept data until a HARD_ERROR is emitted.
- Error envelope: standardize an error response shape (compact) that is machine-readable but includes a short human_message and a remediation_hint. Example envelope fields: code, field_path, severity, human_message, remediation_hint, telemetry_key. We will map existing verbose error strings into this envelope and provide a mapping table for backward compatibility.
- Compatibility layer: orchestrated transforms that run pre-validation. Transforms are ordered, lightweight JS/Py functions or declarative mappings (alias, rename, flatten) that convert v1 shapes to v2. Each transform emits audit events so we can measure conversion success and opt to reject transformed calls under a feature flag.

API changes and runtime integration:
- New endpoint parameter: validation_mode with values {"strict","coerce","suggest"}. Default remains "coerce" for backwards compatibility.
- Streaming protocol: validation events are streamed as top-level event messages with type "validation_event" and payload equal to the compact envelope. Consumers can subscribe to these for realtime UX.
- Backward compatibility: if legacy client does not include validation_mode, runtime uses compatibility transforms + coerce mode and includes telemetry tag "compat_auto_applied": true.

Telemetry and observability: record events for validation_outcome (pass/soft_fail/hard_fail), transform_applied (id), time_to_first_validation_event, and percentage_of_calls_using_streaming_validation. Create new Console dashboard with per-model and per-route breakdowns, and alerts when hard_error rate exceeds 0.5% for production routes.

Trade-offs considered:
- Large schema expressivity vs rollout risk: chose a narrow schema subset to limit unexpected rejects.
- In-stream validation may increase CPU overhead; plan to gate streaming validation by route and sample rate, with autoscaling configs available to customers.
- Human-friendly messages require translations/localization; initial rollout will ship English messages with keys to later add translations.

Open questions:
- What default sampling rate for streaming validation in Hosted to limit cost? (Proposal: 5% for first 2 weeks, then 20% after metrics validation.)
- Should we allow customers to upload custom transforms or only Redwood-managed ones? (Security review requested.)

Acceptance criteria: see acceptance_criteria field.

Rollout plan: staged rollout using runtime-1.20 feature flag. Phase 1: internal Canary (QA + infra) 2 days. Phase 2: selected customers opt-in for compatibility transforms and streaming validation for low-volume routes. Phase 3: broader opt-in with telemetry-based escalation to default coerce behavior only after 4 weeks of stable metrics.
acceptance_criteria: Validator supports streaming mode and emits validation_event messages with the compact envelope
Compatibility transform chain can rename/alias at least 5 legacy fields and emits audit events
Console surface shows new validation metrics and alert rules are configured
Default behavior without validation_mode remains backwards compatible (no increased hard_error rate >0.1%)
Automated unit + integration tests cover soft_error -> suggested_fix mapping and coercion modes
implementation_notes: Schema annotations implemented as JSON Schema $comment-like extension namespaced as x-redwood-*
Validator will be a lightweight library in runtime repo (C++ core + thin TypeScript shim for transforms) to minimize cross-language drift
Expose a small optics API for Console to subscribe to sampled validation_event streams
Start with English human_message keys; use telemetry_key to map to translation pipeline later
security_notes: Transforms will run in sandboxed environment and must be uploaded through signed manifests
Allow-listing: remote customer transforms must be explicitly enabled per-customer and audited
Ensure telemetry keys do not leak PII; field_path in envelopes must use redaction rules for sensitive fields
testing_plan: Unit tests for partial-object validation (prefix/suffix cases)
Integration tests that simulate streaming client sending incremental fields and verify emitted events
Load tests to estimate CPU overhead at 5%, 20%, and 100% sampling rates
Canary on staging with selected production-like routes for 48 hours
